newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Bodos wage decade-long fight for homeland.
newsitem.headline: India's Bodos wage decade-long fight for homeland.

text.p: Bodo tribal guerrillas, suspected of planting a bomb on a train which authorities said killed at least 300 people on Monday, have been fighting for a separate homeland in northeastern India for nearly a decade.
The Bodos are one of many indigenous tribes in hilly northeastern India and among dozens of groups waging violent separatist campaigns across the sprawling country.

Bodos make up about 13 percent of the estimated 25 million people in oil- and tea-rich Assam state, located in a remote section of India which is bordered by Tibet and Bhutan to the north, Burma to the east and Bangladesh to the south and west.

The tribal peoples of Assam, particularly the Bodos centred in Kokrajhar district where Monday's bomb attack occurred, had faced the onslaught of immigrants following the partition of British India in 1947 into mostly Hindu India and Islamic Pakistan.
The animist Bodos have been demanding a separate tribal state north of the Brahmaputra river since the early 1980s, and their campaign took a violent turn at the end of the decade.
At least 1,000 have died in violence related to the Bodo struggle for independence, United News of India said.
The Bodos claim the Assamese have discriminated against them, denying them job opportunities and schools.
They have demanded a separate Bodo state within India to preserve their culture from the Hindu-dominated state government and from the millions of illegal Bangladeshi migrants flooding into the area.
In February 1993, India's federal government signed an accord with moderate Bodos for the formation of the Autonomous Bodoland Area, which was supposed to end the armed insurgency.
But the majority of the Bodo leadership did not accept the peace pact.
Those opposing the pact want hundreds of villages housing Moslems, Bengali Hindus, migrants from Nepal and tea garden workers from elsewhere in Assam incorporated into the autonomous region.
But the state government opposes the inclusion in the autonomous region of any village that has no Bodo population.
Differences over the accord have split the movement, and hard-line militants of the Bodo Security Force (BSF) have unleashed a reign of terror to establish a separate nation.
The BSF has been blamed for murders, extortions and kidnappings and been declared an unlawful organisation.

Over the past two years, authorities had claimed progress in curbing militancy which they said had opened the door to foreign investment in power, roads and other infrastructure projects in the region.
